name: Punk & New Wave
blurb: Three chords, safety pins and the skinny-tie sounds that shook up the late '70s.

questions.prompt: Which New York borough did the Ramones come from?
questions.fact: The four members of the band, from Forest Hills, all took the stage surname Ramone, though none of them were related.

questions.prompt: Which Bowery club, whose name stood for country, bluegrass and blues, launched the Ramones, Television and Blondie?
questions.fact: Owner Hilly Kristal had planned to book country acts, but he ended up hosting the bands that built New York punk.

questions.prompt: Which British band, managed by Malcolm McLaren, released "God Save the Queen" in the week of the 1977 Silver Jubilee?
questions.fact: The BBC refused to play the song, and the band performed it on a boat on the Thames until police ended the party.

questions.prompt: Which band, fronted by Debbie Harry, had hits with "Heart of Glass" and "Call Me"?
questions.fact: "Heart of Glass" began in 1975 as a slower demo called "Once I Had a Love" before the band gave it a disco beat.

questions.prompt: In the 1984 concert film Stop Making Sense, David Byrne wears an enormous what?
questions.fact: Jonathan Demme filmed Talking Heads at the Pantages Theatre in Hollywood, and the oversized suit became the film's best-known image.

questions.prompt: Which Police frontman got his nickname from a black-and-yellow striped sweater?
questions.fact: Gordon Sumner wore the sweater in his jazz-band days, and a bandleader said it made him look like a wasp.

questions.prompt: Which duo of Annie Lennox and Dave Stewart sang "Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This)"?
questions.fact: Lennox and Stewart had earlier been in a band called the Tourists before forming their synthesizer-driven duo.

questions.prompt: Which British band recorded the 1979 double album London Calling?
questions.fact: Producer Guy Stevens was famous for eccentric studio methods, and the album mixed punk with reggae, rockabilly and ska.

questions.prompt: Which American-born singer fronts the British band the Pretenders?
questions.fact: Hynde grew up in Akron, Ohio, moved to London in 1973, and formed the Pretenders in 1978.

questions.prompt: Which Birmingham band's videos for "Hungry Like the Wolf" and "Rio" were filmed in Sri Lanka and Antigua?
questions.fact: The group took its name from a character in the 1968 film Barbarella.

questions.prompt: The cover of London Calling shows Paul Simonon smashing what?
questions.fact: Photographer Pennie Smith took the picture at a New York show in 1979, and the pink and green lettering echoes Elvis Presley's debut album.

questions.prompt: In December 1976 the Sex Pistols swore on live British TV on which program, hosted by Bill Grundy?
questions.fact: Newspapers raged the next day, and the band was soon dropped by its record label, EMI.

questions.prompt: Which photographer shot the cover of Patti Smith's 1975 debut Horses?
questions.fact: Smith and Mapplethorpe had been close friends and housemates in New York, and the album opens with a rewrite of "Gloria".

questions.prompt: Devo's name comes from which idea that humanity was getting dumber instead of smarter?
questions.fact: Founders Mark Mothersbaugh and Jerry Casale met at Kent State, and Casale has said the 1970 shootings there, which he witnessed, shaped the band.

questions.prompt: The B-52's took their name from a slang term for which hairstyle?
questions.fact: The band formed in 1976 after a night at a Chinese restaurant in Athens, Georgia, where they drank a flaming volcano bowl and then jammed.

questions.prompt: Which former Roxy Music member produced Talking Heads' Fear of Music and Remain in Light?
questions.fact: Remain in Light, from 1980, drew on Afrobeat and the music of Fela Kuti.

questions.prompt: After the death of singer Ian Curtis in 1980, the surviving members of Joy Division regrouped as which band?
questions.fact: Joy Division had been about to leave for its first American tour when Curtis died.

questions.prompt: Sting wrote "Every Breath You Take" at which famous location in Jamaica?
questions.fact: Sting has said the song's melody and words came to him in the middle of the night at the desk where Fleming wrote his James Bond novels.

questions.prompt: What was Elvis Costello's birth name?
questions.fact: His 1977 debut, My Aim Is True, was recorded with an American band called Clover.

questions.prompt: Patti Smith's "Because the Night" was co-written with which rock star?
questions.fact: Springsteen had a demo of the music, which reached Smith through producer Jimmy Iovine, and she wrote the words herself.

questions.prompt: The Ramones' 1976 debut album was recorded for roughly how much?
questions.fact: The album was made in about a week and sold modestly at first, but it inspired countless bands, especially in Britain.

questions.prompt: Joe Strummer fronted which pub-rock band before joining the Clash?
questions.fact: The band took its name from a squat at 101 Walterton Road in London.

questions.prompt: Paul Weller broke up the Jam in 1982 at the height of its fame to form which band?
questions.fact: Weller teamed with keyboardist Mick Talbot and moved toward soul and jazz sounds.

questions.prompt: Siouxsie and the Banshees' first single, "Hong Kong Garden", was inspired by what?
questions.fact: Siouxsie has said she was thinking of the staff at the takeaway, who were harassed by skinheads.

questions.prompt: Which producer, known for Sweet and Suzi Quatro hits, produced Blondie's Parallel Lines?
questions.fact: Chapman demanded dozens of takes to get the band's sound just right.

questions.prompt: Which producer who worked with Queen made The Cars' 1978 debut album?
questions.fact: The glossy, layered sound made the Boston band a success on radio and early MTV.

questions.prompt: Which Television co-founder left in 1975 and later formed the Voidoids?
questions.fact: His torn shirts and spiky hair are said to have influenced Malcolm McLaren's look for the Sex Pistols.

questions.prompt: Which band released "New Rose" in October 1976, the first British punk single?
questions.fact: The Damned beat the Pistols to a record by a few weeks, and they were also the first British punk band to tour America.

questions.prompt: Which Clash member wrote the music for "Rock the Casbah" and played most of the instruments?
questions.fact: Strummer wrote the lyrics after Headon had recorded the music on his own.

questions.prompt: The Cure's first single, "Killing an Arab", was inspired by a novel by which author?
questions.fact: Robert Smith has said it was an existential tale, not a political statement, and the band later added disclaimers to reissues.

stories.title: CBGB and the Ramones
stories.dek: Four leather jackets and a very small club
stories.body:
In 1973 a former Marine named Hilly Kristal opened a small club at 315 Bowery in lower Manhattan. He named it CBGB OMFUG, which stood for Country, Bluegrass, Blues and Other Music for Uplifting Gormandizers. He planned to host country music. The Bowery in those years was a rough neighborhood of flophouses and empty storefronts, and the country crowd never came. Instead, young bands with nowhere else to play began to fill the room.

One of them came from Forest Hills, a quiet middle-class neighborhood in Queens. Four friends, Joey, Johnny, Dee Dee and Tommy, took the stage surname Ramone and wore the same uniform of torn jeans, sneakers and black leather jackets. They played fast. Each song was short, and each began with Dee Dee shouting a count of "one, two, three, four", as if the band could not wait. They played their first show at CBGB in August 1974 and returned again and again.

The sets were short, often around twenty minutes, and the crowd was small. But other musicians were watching. Patti Smith, Television, Blondie and Talking Heads were all playing the same stage in those years, and together they made a scene. Critics began to write about it. In 1976 the Ramones made their first album for a few thousand dollars, and the opening track, "Blitzkrieg Bop", gave the new music one of its first anthems.

The band's real influence landed across the ocean. On July 4, 1976, the Ramones played at the Roundhouse in London. In the audience were young musicians who would soon become the Clash, the Sex Pistols and the Damned. They saw a band that played with no solos, no flashy show and no fear. The message was clear: anyone could do this. Within months, British punk bands were forming everywhere.

At home the Ramones never had a big hit, though they kept touring for twenty years. Their influence did the work. Bands as varied as the Clash, Metallica and Green Day have all credited them as an influence.

CBGB lasted until 2006, covered in stickers and posters, and its fame outlasted the bands that made it. Hilly Kristal had set out to book country and blues, and he ended up hosting the sound that would change rock and roll.

stories.title: The Pistols and the Jubilee
stories.dek: A boat on the Thames and a song the BBC would not play
stories.body:
The Sex Pistols were put together in London in 1975 by Malcolm McLaren, who ran a clothing shop on the King's Road. He had spent time in New York and saw the New York Dolls, and he wanted to bring that raw spirit to Britain. The band's lead singer was a sneering teenager named John Lydon, nicknamed Johnny Rotten, and the bassist was Glen Matlock. They signed with EMI in 1976.

Then came December. The band appeared on a teatime TV show called Today, where host Bill Grundy, apparently trying to provoke them, goaded the band into swearing live on air. The next day the tabloids raged. Concerts were canceled, and EMI dropped the band. Matlock left and was replaced by Sid Vicious, a friend of Lydon's who could barely play the bass. A&M Records signed them in March 1977 in a ceremony outside Buckingham Palace, then dropped them within a week. Finally Virgin Records, under Richard Branson, took a chance.

In May Virgin released "God Save the Queen". The timing was deliberate. Britain was preparing to celebrate Queen Elizabeth's Silver Jubilee, twenty-five years on the throne, and here was a song that sneered at the monarchy. The BBC refused to play it, and many shops would not stock it. On June 7, during the Jubilee week, McLaren hired a boat to carry the band along the Thames past the Houses of Parliament. They played the song on deck. Police boats closed in, the party was stopped, and several people were arrested.

The single sold hundreds of thousands of copies and reached No. 2 on the UK chart. Many fans are convinced it was kept from the top spot, but the Official Charts lists it at No. 2, behind a Rod Stewart single. The band's only studio album, Never Mind the Bollocks, followed in October.

The Pistols did not last. After a chaotic tour of the United States, they broke up in January 1978 at a show in San Francisco, where Lydon asked the audience if they ever got the feeling they had been cheated. Vicious died of an overdose in 1979, at the age of 21.

The band had lasted barely two years. But its anger, its look and its three chords had given a whole generation permission to start a band of their own.

stories.title: Joy Division and New Order
stories.dek: A Manchester band that became two bands
stories.body:
In 1976 two friends from Salford, Bernard Sumner and Peter Hook, saw the Sex Pistols play in Manchester. Hook borrowed money from his mother to buy a bass. They found a drummer, Stephen Morris, and a singer named Ian Curtis, and they called themselves Joy Division. The band signed to a new local label, Factory Records, whose co-founder was television presenter Tony Wilson.

In 1979 they recorded their first album, Unknown Pleasures, in Stockport with a producer named Martin Hannett. He had a particular idea of sound. He wanted a cold, spacious record with drums that echoed in an empty room. The songs were dark and spare, and Curtis sang them in a deep, trembling baritone. The cover, designed by Peter Saville, showed a black field with white wavy lines. It was a picture of the radio pulses from a distant star, taken from an astronomy book, and it appeared with no title or band name. It became one of the most copied sleeves in rock.

Curtis suffered from epilepsy and from depression. He wrote about isolation and anxiety, and sometimes had seizures on stage. In 1980 the band was preparing for its first American tour. On May 18, the day before they were to leave, Curtis took his own life at his home in Macclesfield. He was 23. A few weeks later Factory released a single they had recorded earlier, "Love Will Tear Us Apart". It became their best-known song and their biggest hit.

The three survivors decided to continue. They chose a new name, New Order, and added keyboardist Gillian Gilbert. At first they struggled to find their voice. Sumner took over vocals, and the band began to experiment with synthesizers, drum machines and dance rhythms.

In 1983 they released "Blue Monday", a long, pulsing track built on electronic beats. It was a hit in clubs and on the radio, and it is often called the best-selling 12-inch single of all time. The band and Factory also opened a nightclub in Manchester, the Haçienda, which became a center of British dance culture.

Joy Division had made one of the most haunting records in rock. New Order took the same people into a different world, and both bands remain among the most influential of the era.

stories.title: The Gig That Started Manchester
stories.dek: The Sex Pistols play a small hall in June 1976.
stories.body:
On June 4, 1976, the Sex Pistols played a show at the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester. The band was less than a year old and had made a name for itself in London with loud, rude and chaotic shows, but it was not yet famous in the north of England. The concert was organized by two local students, Howard Devoto and Pete Shelley, who had formed a band called Buzzcocks and who had traveled to London to see the Pistols play. They liked what they saw and decided to bring them to Manchester.

The audience was small. According to the usual account, there were about forty people in the room, and many of them did not know what to expect. The Pistols played with their usual attitude, loud and fast and not caring whether the crowd approved. Johnny Rotten stood at the front, and the band played songs that were short, angry and funny.

What made the night remarkable is who was there, and what they did afterward. Many of the people in the audience reportedly went on to form bands or play major roles in the music scene. They included members of the future Joy Division, Ian Curtis, Peter Hook and Bernard Sumner, along with Morrissey, who would front the Smiths, and Mark E. Smith, who would lead the Fall. Tony Wilson, a television presenter who would co-found Factory Records, is also said to have attended. Whether or not every name on the list is accurate, the point is that the show seemed to light a fuse.

The Pistols returned to the same hall on July 20, and this time the Buzzcocks opened. The crowd was bigger, and the scene in Manchester had begun to form. Devoto and Shelley's band put out its first record, Spiral Scratch, in early 1977, on its own label, a bold move that showed other bands that they did not need a major record company.

Many of the groups that came after the Pistols' visit, from Joy Division to the Smiths, wrote about the city's gray streets and everyday feelings. The Pistols had arrived with songs of rage, such as God Save the Queen, which came out in 1977. The musicians in Manchester heard the same urgency, and they used it in their own ways.

The show is sometimes described as the gig that changed everything. It was a small hall, a few dozen people and a band that did not care. That was enough.

stories.title: Rock Against Racism in Victoria Park
stories.dek: A carnival in East London, April 30, 1978.
stories.body:
Rock Against Racism began in 1976 after a bad night. Eric Clapton, one of Britain's best-known guitarists, said some things on stage in Birmingham that appeared to support the politician Enoch Powell's views on immigration. A group of musicians and activists, including photographer Red Saunders, wrote an angry letter to the music press, and the response was strong enough that a movement was born. Its aim was to use music to counter racism in Britain, and it organized concerts around the country.

By the spring of 1978 the movement was ready for a big public event. On April 30, supporters marched from Trafalgar Square in central London to Victoria Park in the East End, where a free carnival was held. Estimates of the crowd range from about eighty thousand to a hundred thousand.

The lineup was a mix of punk, reggae and rock bands, which was exactly the point. The Tom Robinson Band, X-Ray Spex, Steel Pulse, a reggae band from Birmingham, and the Clash were among the acts. The Clash were at the center of punk's growing connection with reggae. They played hard and fast, and their set included White Riot, one of the best-known songs from their first album. Many in the crowd, white and Black, sang along.

The carnival showed that punk was more than a fashion or a shout of rebellion. Many bands wanted their music to say something about the world, and the Clash in particular wrote about unemployment, police and politics. Late in 1979, they would release London Calling, an album that merged punk with reggae, rockabilly and soul, and the title song became one of the group's best known.

Rock Against Racism continued to organize events through the late 1970s and into the 1980s, and its message of unity reached a wide audience. It is often credited with helping to shape the culture of the time.

The Victoria Park carnival is remembered for its size, but it also stands for something simple. A crowd of young people from many backgrounds stood together in a park, listening to music that spoke for them.
